summary: In microgravity, the absence of buoyancy-driven convection fundamentally alters fire physics: flames form spherical fronts, burn at lower temperatures, and propagate via molecular diffusion and subtle spacecraft ventilation currents. Developed by InSpace Creators for the "Flame in Freefall" challenge, PyroMicro-SI is an SI-powered analytical pipeline and interactive safety framework built on NASA’s Physical Science Informatics (PSI) repository. By standardizing heterogeneous experimental records from ISS combustion investigations (FLEX, BASS, and Saffire) into strict International System of Units (SI) metrics—Kelvin (K), Pascals (Pa), meters per second (m/s), and watts per square meter (W/m²)—our solution extracts quantitative flame-spread rates, droplet burning constants, and cool-flame transition boundaries. PyroMicro-SI empowers spacecraft engineers to model flammability thresholds under lunar and Martian exploration atmospheres and optimize fire detection and suppression protocols for future crewed missions.
details:
Overview & Problem Statement

Fire safety is one of the most critical operational risks in human spaceflight. In Earth’s 1g environment, buoyant convection lifts hot combustion products upward, drawing fresh oxygen into the base of a flame. In microgravity (µg), buoyancy vanishes. Flames become spherical, radiative heat loss dominates, and low-velocity cabin HVAC airflows (0.01 to 0.20 m/s) govern oxygen transport. Furthermore, microgravity experiments aboard the International Space Station (ISS) revealed the existence of self-sustaining "cool flames" (600–800 K)—invisible, low-temperature combustion regimes that produce toxic partial-oxidation gases (such as carbon monoxide and formaldehyde) and threaten delayed re-ignition.

While NASA’s Physical Science Informatics (PSI) database houses decades of microgravity combustion telemetry, researchers and habitat engineers face a data standardization bottleneck: experimental logs span disparate legacy units, unindexed high-speed imaging frames, and varied environmental chambers.

Our Solution: PyroMicro-SI

InSpace Creators developed PyroMicro-SI, an SI-standardized data analysis framework and predictive safety insight tool that converts raw NASA PSI microgravity combustion records into actionable engineering parameters:

1. Automated SI Unit Normalization Pipeline:

All ingested experimental variables across droplet and solid-fuel datasets are harmonized into strict SI units:

- Ambient & Flame Temperatures: Kelvin (K)

- Cabin / Chamber Pressure: Pascals (Pa / kPa)

- Forced Ventilation Flow Velocity: Meters per second (m/s)

- Fuel Geometry & Flame Spread Velocity: Millimeters (mm) and Millimeters per second (mm/s)

- Radiative Heat Flux: Watts per square meter (W/m^2)

- Oxygen Mole Fraction: Dimensionless molar ratio (mol/mol)

2. Quantitative Combustion Modeling (d^2 - Law & Spread Kinetics):

Using droplet radius time-series from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX), PyroMicro-SI evaluates the classic d^2b- law of droplet combustion (d^2(t) = d_0^2 - K/t) in SI units (mm^2/s) to isolate the burning rate constant K, radiative extinction diameter, and transition point to diffusive cool-flame regimes.

3. Key Spacecraft Fire Safety Insights:

- The Ventilation Sweet-Spot Hazard: Cross-analyzing BASS (Burning and Suppression of Solids) and Saffire datasets demonstrates that while solid fuels often self-extinguish in stagnant microgravity air due to local oxygen starvation shell formation, concurrent cabin ventilation flows of just 0.05 to 0.12 m/s maximize flame spread rate and prevent radiative quenching. Immediately cutting cabin HVAC fans upon optical smoke/flame detection is the single fastest non-chemical suppression action.

- Exploration Atmosphere Trade-Offs (Artemis / Mars Transit): Evaluating NASA’s proposed hypoxic, higher-oxygen exploration atmosphere 56.5 kPa total pressure at 34% against standard ISS sea-level conditions (101.3 kPa at 21%) shows a ~28% increase in opposed-flow flame propagation speed mm/s and a lower minimum ignition energy (J), requiring recalibrated ultraviolet/infrared (UV/IR) optical sensor thresholds.

- Cool-Flame Post-Suppression Monitoring: Because heptane and alkane droplets transition into invisible cool flames (~650 K) after visible hot-flame radiative extinction (~1400 K), spacecraft post-fire protocols must maintain inert gas (CO_2/N_2) enrichment and catalytic filtration until thermal and spectroscopic sensors confirm zero partial-oxidation emissions.
